main.claim: Choose your image, click any spot, and the color appears as HEX, RGB and HSL. Click a code to copy it, or extract a 6-color palette from the picture. Free, in your browser, and nothing is uploaded.

sections.heading: How to pick a color from an image
sections.body:
Open [Color Picker](https://color-picker.lazur.app/) on your computer or phone. You can load a picture in two ways: click **Choose image** and pick the file, or drag the image straight onto the dashed box. The picture appears at once.

1. Load your image with Choose image, or drag it onto the box.
2. Click the spot whose color you want. On a computer, hover first to see a magnified view of the pixels under your pointer.
3. Read the color as HEX, RGB and HSL. A swatch shows the color you picked, next to the codes.
4. Click any code to copy it.

Each click picks a new color and adds it to your recent colors, so you can compare two spots without losing the first one.

sections.heading: What the three codes mean
sections.body:
**HEX** is a color written as a # sign and six letters or numbers, like #FF8800. Websites, CSS and most design apps read this form. **RGB** lists the amounts of red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255. **HSL** lists hue, saturation and lightness. It is the easiest form when you want a lighter or darker version of the same color.

Use HEX when you paste into a website or a design file. Use RGB or HSL when an app asks for those values, or when you plan to adjust the shade by hand.

sections.heading: Build a palette from the picture
sections.body:
Click **Extract palette** and the tool finds six main colors in the image, each with its HEX code. A photo of a sunset, a logo or a product shot gives you a useful set. Click a swatch to copy its code, or click **Copy palette** to copy all six codes at once, separated by commas.

Use the palette to match a poster, a slide deck or a social post to a photo. Start with the color that covers the most of the picture, then choose one lighter or darker color for headings and one accent for buttons.

sections.heading: Fixes when the picker does not open your image
sections.body:
If you see **That doesn't look like an image**, the file is not a picture format the browser reads. Save a copy as PNG or JPG from your photo app and load that copy. If you see **Couldn't open that image**, the file may be damaged or incomplete. Export it again, or download it again, and then load it.

The codes change only when you click. Click a flat area in the middle of the color you want, not a shadow or a bright edge.

sections.heading: Your image stays on your device
sections.body:
Nothing is uploaded. Your browser reads the picture, so you do not need an account, an app or a sign-up. Recent colors stay on the page only until you close it or load a new image.

If you spend your day in design files and documents, Lazur on your Mac lets you hold two keys and talk. It types for you in whatever app you are in, at [lazur.app](https://www.lazur.app).

sections.heading: How to get the hex code from a picture
sections.body:
Open the [color picker](https://color-picker.lazur.app/hex-code). The steps take less than a minute, and you do not need an account.

1. Click **Choose image** and pick your picture, or drag it onto the dashed box.
2. Click the spot whose color you need.
3. Find the code that starts with a # sign. That is the HEX code.
4. Click the code to copy it, then paste it where you need it.

The HEX code sits in a chip beside the swatch. Once you click it, the code is on your clipboard, ready to paste into a design file, a CSS file or a brand guide.

sections.heading: What a hex code is
sections.body:
A hex code is a color written as a # sign and six characters. Each pair of characters stands for one part of the color. The first pair is red, the second is green and the third is blue. Each pair runs from 00 to FF, which means 0 to 255 in plain numbers. So #FF0000 is pure red, #000000 is black and #FFFFFF is white.

Hex is the form most websites use in CSS, and most design apps accept it too. If an app asks for RGB instead, the same color is in the RGB chip next to the HEX code, so you can copy that one.

sections.heading: Click the exact pixel
sections.body:
On a computer, move your pointer over the image. A round magnifier shows the pixels under the pointer, with the one you are about to pick outlined in the middle. Move until the outlined pixel sits on the color you want, then click.

Pick from the middle of a flat area. Edges and highlights blend two colors, so the code from an edge may not match the color you see across the whole object. Click two or three spots in the same area and compare the codes. If they match, you have a reliable color. If they differ, the photo has shading, so use the code from the spot that looks most like the true color.

On a phone, there is no hover, so tap the middle of the area and then tap once more nearby to check the code.

sections.heading: Keep your colors and reuse them
sections.body:
The last 10 colors you picked stay in **Recent colors** under the image. Tap or click one to copy its HEX code again, without finding the spot a second time.

The list clears when you close the page or load a new image. Copy any code you want to keep before you move on, and paste it into a note or a file.

sections.heading: Why a photo code can look off
sections.body:
A photo is not a flat color chart. Light, shadows and camera settings all shift the colors a little. JPG files also throw away some color detail to make the file smaller, so a JPG can give a slightly different code from the original. Save or export a PNG when you have one, because PNG keeps the original pixel values.

If the code still looks wrong, pick a different flat spot, compare two codes, and choose the one that matches the color you see in real life.

sections.heading: Nothing is uploaded
sections.body: The image is read in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, and no account or app is needed. If you see **That doesn't look like an image**, the file is not in a picture format the browser reads. Export it as PNG or JPG and try again.

faq.q: How do I get a hex code from an image?
faq.a: Open the color picker, choose your image, and click the spot you want. The HEX code appears in a chip beside the swatch, starting with a # sign. Click the code to copy it. Nothing is uploaded, and no account is needed.

faq.q: Can I get a hex code from a photo on my phone?
faq.a: Yes. Open the page in your phone's browser, tap Choose image, and pick the photo. Then tap the spot you want. Tap the HEX code to copy it. There is no app to install, and the photo is read in your browser.

faq.q: Why does the same color show a different hex code?
faq.a: Photos change colors. Lighting, shadows, camera settings and JPG compression all shift the values a little. Pick the middle of a flat area, click two or three spots to compare, and use a PNG when you can, because PNG keeps the original pixel values.

faq.q: Is the hex code picker free?
faq.a: Yes. The picker runs in your browser and needs no sign-up. Nothing is uploaded, so the picture stays on your device while you work.

sections.heading: Pick a color from an image on your Mac
sections.body:
Open the [color picker for Mac](https://color-picker.lazur.app/mac) in the browser you already use. Then load the image.

1. Drag the image from Finder onto the dashed box. Or click **Choose image** and pick the file in the Mac window that opens.
2. Click the spot you want. Hover first to see a magnified view under the pointer.
3. Read the HEX, RGB and HSL codes.
4. Click a code to copy it, then paste it into Pages, Keynote or any other app.

You do not need to save the picture anywhere special. Use the file where it already lives on your Mac, and the image loads in the page.

sections.heading: Drag a file from Finder
sections.body:
Dragging works well when the image is a file in Finder, such as a screenshot on your Desktop or a photo in Downloads. Hold the file and move it over the dashed box. The box changes color while the file is over it. Let go, and the picture appears.

If the box does not respond, click **Choose image** instead and pick the same file. Both ways load the picture the same way, so the codes you get are identical.

Dragging also works for a file you just saved from a website or a screenshot. You do not need to rename it or move it into a folder first. Drop it on the box, and check that the picture on screen matches the one you meant before you click.

sections.heading: Digital Color Meter reads your screen, not image files
sections.body:
macOS includes an app called Digital Color Meter. Apple's guide says it finds the color value of a color on your screen. Use it when the color is on your display, such as a website you cannot save or a window you cannot drag a file out of.

The guide describes sampling colors from the screen. It does not describe opening a saved image file, so use this page for pictures you already have. For a color on screen, open [Digital Color Meter](https://support.apple.com/guide/digital-color-meter/welcome/mac) and follow Apple's guide.

sections.heading: Copy and use the codes
sections.body:
Each code in the tool has its own copy action. Click HEX, RGB or HSL to copy that value. After you extract a palette, **Copy palette** copies the six HEX codes separated by commas, which is handy when a design app asks for a list.

Click a single palette swatch to copy just that code. Paste it into Pages, Keynote, a document or a design file, and check the color against the original before you print or publish.

sections.heading: Privacy on your Mac
sections.body: The image is read in your browser on your Mac. Nothing is uploaded, and the tool does not ask you to sign up or install anything. Recent colors stay on the page only until you close it or load a new image.

faq.q: How do I pick a color from an image on a Mac?
faq.a: Open the color picker in your browser, drag your image from Finder onto the dashed box, and click the spot you want. The HEX, RGB and HSL codes appear. Click any code to copy it. You can also use Choose image to pick the file.

faq.q: Does a Mac have a color picker for image files?
faq.a: macOS has Digital Color Meter, but Apple's guide describes it for colors on your screen. To read a color from a saved image file, use this page: load the file, then click the pixel you want.

faq.q: Can I get a palette from a photo on a Mac?
faq.a: Yes. After the image loads, click Extract palette. The tool shows six main colors from the picture, each with its HEX code. Click a swatch to copy its code, or click Copy palette to copy all six.

faq.q: Do I need to install anything on my Mac?
faq.a: No. The color picker runs in your browser, so there is no app to download and no sign-up. Nothing is uploaded, so the image stays on your Mac while you work.

sections.heading: Pick a color from a photo on iPhone
sections.body:
Open the [color picker on iPhone](https://color-picker.lazur.app/iphone) in Safari or any other browser on your phone. No app is needed.

1. Tap **Choose image** and pick the photo from your phone.
2. Tap the spot you want. The color appears in the swatch with its codes.
3. Tap the HEX code to copy it.
4. Paste it into Notes, Messages or the app where you need it.

The photo is read on your iPhone while you work. Nothing is uploaded.

sections.heading: Tap the middle of a flat area
sections.body:
An iPhone has no mouse, so you cannot hover to see a magnified view. The photo is scaled to fit your screen width, which makes small details harder to hit with a finger. Tap the middle of the area that shows your color, then tap a second spot close by.

If the two codes match, use either one. If they differ, the photo has shading there, so tap a flatter part of the object. Compare two or three taps before you choose the code for a design.

Pictures you take with the camera work the same way as screenshots, because the picker only needs the image file. To check a color on a website, take a screenshot first and save it to your photo library. Then choose that screenshot in the picker. Tap the spot in a solid part of the color, not on the text or the edge of a button, so the code matches the color you meant.

sections.heading: Copy the code and keep it
sections.body:
Tap any code to copy it. The code shows a check mark for a moment, so you know the copy worked. Recent colors appear under the image as small round swatches. Tap one to copy its HEX code again.

The recent list clears when you close the page or load a new image. Paste the code into a note or message before you move on, so you keep it.

sections.heading: When the picker says it couldn't open your image
sections.body:
If you see **Couldn't open that image**, the file loaded but the browser could not read it. Save or export a copy as a JPG or PNG, then choose that copy again.

If you see **That doesn't look like an image**, the file is not a picture at all. Choose a photo instead of a document or a video. The picker reads the common picture formats, such as PNG, JPG, WebP and GIF.

sections.heading: Nothing is uploaded
sections.body: The color picker reads the photo in your browser. Nothing is uploaded, and no app, account or sign-up is needed. If you close the page and open it again, it starts fresh with no photo loaded.

faq.q: How do I get a color code from a photo on my iPhone?
faq.a: Open the color picker in your browser, tap Choose image, and pick the photo. Tap the spot you want. The HEX, RGB and HSL codes appear, and tapping a code copies it. The photo is read on your phone and is not uploaded.

faq.q: Do I need to download an app to pick colors on iPhone?
faq.a: No. The color picker runs in the browser on your iPhone, so you open a page and pick a photo. Nothing is installed, and no account or sign-up is needed.

faq.q: Why does the picker say it couldn't open my image?
faq.a: The file may be damaged, or the browser may not read that format. Save or export a copy as a JPG or PNG, then choose it again. If you see a message that the file does not look like an image, pick a photo instead.

sections.heading: Four steps to pick a color from any image
sections.body:
Open the [color picker](https://color-picker.lazur.app/pick) on any device, then follow these steps.

1. Load the picture with **Choose image**, or drag it onto the box.
2. Click the spot you want. The color appears in a large swatch.
3. Read the HEX, RGB or HSL code under the swatch.
4. Click the code to copy it.

That is all you need for one color. For more colors, use the recent colors list or the palette below the image.

If the color is on a website, take a screenshot first, then load the screenshot. The picker reads a saved image, so it can only sample what is in the file you load.

sections.heading: Choose the spot that matches the color
sections.body:
The color you see in a photo is rarely one flat value. Light falls on one side of an object and not the other, so two spots that look the same to you can have slightly different codes.

Click the middle of the area that shows the color best, then click again near it. If the codes match, you can trust them. If they differ, choose the one from the most even part of the object. Avoid shadows, glare and the edges where two colors meet.

sections.heading: What the codes say
sections.body:
**HEX** is six characters after a # sign, like #FF0000 for pure red. **RGB** gives red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255. **HSL** gives hue, saturation and lightness.

Use HEX for websites and CSS, and RGB or HSL for apps that ask for those numbers. HSL is the easiest form when you want a lighter or darker shade of the same color, because you change only the lightness number.

sections.heading: Get a palette from the same image
sections.body:
Click **Extract palette** under the image. The tool finds six main colors and shows each one with its HEX code. Click a swatch to copy its code. Click **Copy palette** to copy all six codes, separated by commas.

A palette works well for a slide deck, a thumbnail or a poster that should match a photo. Pick the color that covers the most of the picture for the main background, then one accent for buttons or headings.

sections.heading: When the picker shows an error
sections.body:
**That doesn't look like an image** means the file is not a picture format the browser reads. Export it as a PNG, JPG, WebP or GIF, then load it again.

**Couldn't open that image** means the file loaded but the browser could not read it. The file may be damaged, so try another copy.

sections.heading: Your image stays on your device
sections.body: Nothing is uploaded. The image is read in your browser, so you do not need an account or an app. Your recent colors stay on the page only until you close it or load a new image.

faq.q: How can I identify a color from an image?
faq.a: Load the image in the color picker and click the spot you want. The tool shows the color as HEX, RGB and HSL codes. It gives you the codes, not a color name, so use those codes to match the color in your design app.

faq.q: Is there a free tool that can identify colors from an image?
faq.a: Yes. This color picker is free, runs in your browser and needs no sign-up. You can pick a color from any spot, copy its codes, or extract a palette of six colors. Nothing is uploaded.

faq.q: How do I pick a color from a photo on my iPhone?
faq.a: Open the color picker in your phone's browser, tap Choose image, and pick the photo. Tap the spot you want, then tap a code to copy it. There is no app to install, and the photo is read in your browser.
